claim: 204 new historical period genomes were collected from Europe and the Mediterranean from 53 archaeological sites in 18 countries.
source: We collected whole genomes from 204 individuals across 53 archaeological sites in 18 countries spanning Europe and the Mediterranean (Figure 1—figure supplement 1), 26 of these individuals were recently reported (Moots et al., 2022).
evidence: Directly stated in the manuscript text describing the sample collection.

claim: 26 of the 204 individuals were recently reported in Moots et al., 2022.
source: We collected whole genomes from 204 individuals across 53 archaeological sites in 18 countries spanning Europe and the Mediterranean (Figure 1—figure supplement 1), 26 of these individuals were recently reported (Moots et al., 2022).
evidence: Directly stated with citation to previous publication.

claim: The collection includes the first historical genomes from present-day Armenia, Algeria, Austria, and France.
source: This collection includes the first historical genomes (Iron Age and later, i.e. after 1000 BCE) from present-day Armenia, Algeria, Austria, and France.
evidence: Explicitly stated in the manuscript text.

claim: DNA was extracted from the powdered cochlear portion of the petrous bone for 203 samples.
source: DNA was extracted from either the powdered cochlear portion of the petrous bone (n=203) or from teeth (n=1).
evidence: Directly stated in the methods section.

claim: DNA was extracted from teeth for 1 sample.
source: DNA was extracted from either the powdered cochlear portion of the petrous bone (n=203) or from teeth (n=1).
evidence: Directly stated in the methods section.

claim: Whole genome sequencing was performed to a median depth of 0.92x (range 0.16x to 2.38x).
source: We performed whole genome sequencing to a median depth of 0.92 x (0.16x to 2.38x).
evidence: Directly stated sequencing depth statistics.

claim: Pseudohaploid genotypes were called for the 1240k SNP panel, resulting in a median of 685,058 SNPs (167,000–1,029,345) per sample.
source: For downstream integration with published data, pseudohaploid genotypes were called for the 1240 k SNP panel (Mathieson et al., 2015), resulting in a median of 685,058 SNPs (167,000–1,029,345) per sample.
evidence: Directly stated genotyping results.

claim: Newly reported genomes were analyzed in conjunction with 2033 present-day genomes, 1998 prehistoric genomes, and 764 published historical period genomes.
source: We analyzed newly reported genomes in conjunction with 2033 present-day genomes, 1998 prehistoric genomes, and 764 published historical period genomes (Clemente et al., 2021; Kovacevic et al., 2014, Mallick et al., 2023; Pagani et al., 2016; Saupe et al., 2021; Žegarac et al., 2021, primary AADR sources cited in Materials and methods).
evidence: Directly stated sample sizes with citations.

claim: Most present-day European genomes can be modeled as a three-way mixture of Western Hunter-Gatherers, Neolithic farmers, and Bronze Age Herders from the Steppe.
source: As a result, most present-day European genomes can be modeled as a three-way mixture of these prehistoric groups: Western Hunter-Gatherers, Neolithic farmers, and Bronze Age Herders from the Steppe (Haak et al., 2015; Lazaridis et al., 2014) with minor contributions from other groups (Antonio et al., 2019; Fernandes et al., 2020; Lazaridis et al., 2016; Morrison et al., 2020; Mathieson et al., 2018).
evidence: Stated with multiple supporting citations.

claim: The genetic structure of Europe mirrors its geography.
source: These ancestry components are present at different proportions across western Eurasia, leading to a pattern where the genetic structure of Europe mirrors its geography (Novembre et al., 2008).
evidence: Stated with citation to Novembre et al., 2008.

claim: The city of Rome harbored a large diversity of ancestries from across Europe and the Mediterranean from the Iron Age through the Imperial Roman period.
source: In the city of Rome alone, the population was dynamic and harbored a large diversity of ancestries from across Europe and the Mediterranean from the Iron Age (~1000 BCE) through the Imperial Roman period (27 BCE-300 CE; Antonio et al., 2019).
evidence: Stated with citation to Antonio et al., 2019.

claim: Historical genomes from the Iberian Peninsula highlight gene flow from across the Mediterranean.
source: Historical genomes from the Iberian Peninsula also highlight gene flow from across the Mediterranean (Olalde et al., 2019).
evidence: Stated with citation to Olalde et al., 2019.

claim: By the Iron Age, sea travel was already common, enabling peoples from across the Mediterranean to come into contact for trade.
source: By the Iron Age, sea travel was already common, enabling peoples from across the Mediterranean to come into contact for trade (Abulafia, 2011; Broodbank, 2013).
evidence: Stated with citations to historical sources.

claim: The Roman Empire built upon existing waterways and roads throughout Europe and created a united Mediterranean for the only time in history.
source: Subsequently, the Roman Empire leveraged its organization, labor force, and military prowess to build upon existing waterways and roads throughout Europe and create a united Mediterranean for the only time in history (Beard, 2015; Harper, 2017; Symonds, 2017).
evidence: Stated with citations to historical sources.

claim: A majority of regions have highly heterogeneous populations in at least one historical time period.
source: A majority of regions have highly heterogeneous populations in at least one historical time period (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Stated with reference to figure showing heterogeneity.

claim: On average, 10 genetic clusters were identified within each region present during the historical period, with a minimum of two and a maximum of 23.
source: On average, we identified 10 genetic clusters within each region present during the historical period, with a minimum of two and a maximum of 23.
evidence: Directly stated statistical summary of clustering analysis.

claim: In Armenia, the population is highly homogeneous at any given time.
source: In Armenia, for example, the population is highly homogeneous at any given time (Figure 2).
evidence: Stated with reference to Figure 2.

claim: After the Copper Age in Armenia, there are two distinct genetic clusters, separated by a temporal split around 772–403 BCE.
source: After the Copper Age, there are two distinct genetic clusters, separated by a temporal split around 772–403 BCE (Figure 2BC).
evidence: Stated with reference to Figure 2BC showing temporal split.

claim: The earlier Armenian cluster (C1) includes 5 newly reported samples from Beniamin and 6 published samples from five other sites.
source: The earlier cluster (C1) includes newly reported samples (n=5) from Beniamin and published ones (n=6) from five other sites.
evidence: Directly stated sample composition of cluster.

claim: The earlier Armenian cluster (C1) cannot be modeled by any single source of ancestry using existing data.
source: This cluster cannot be modeled by any single source of ancestry using existing data.
evidence: Directly stated result of admixture modeling.

claim: The later Armenian cluster (C3) contains 12 newly reported samples from Beniamin dating between 403 BCE-500 CE.
source: The later cluster (C3), which contains newly reported samples (n=12) from Beniamin dating between 403 BCE-500 CE, is genetically similar to present-day Armenians (excluding two Kurdish individuals; Figure 2C).
evidence: Directly stated sample composition and dating.

claim: The later Armenian cluster (C3) is genetically similar to present-day Armenians (excluding two Kurdish individuals).
source: The later cluster (C3), which contains newly reported samples (n=12) from Beniamin dating between 403 BCE-500 CE, is genetically similar to present-day Armenians (excluding two Kurdish individuals; Figure 2C).
evidence: Stated with reference to Figure 2C showing PCA.

claim: The later Armenian cluster (C3) can be modeled using around 50% of the earlier cluster (C1) and an additional source of Steppe ancestry.
source: Despite the split, there is evidence of partial continuity between the earlier and later clusters: the later (C3) can be modeled using around 50% of the earlier cluster (C1) and an additional source of Steppe ancestry.
evidence: Directly stated result of admixture modeling.

claim: Historical genomes from Northern Europe, particularly from Lithuania and Poland, exhibit a similar level of homogeneity to Armenia.
source: Historical genomes from Northern Europe, particularly newly reported genomes from Lithuania and Poland, exhibit a similar level of homogeneity (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Stated with reference to supplementary figure.

claim: Most regions including Italy, Southeastern Europe, and Western Europe had strikingly heterogeneous populations.
source: In contrast to the homogeneity of the Armenian population, most of the regions, including Italy, Southeastern Europe, and Western Europe, had strikingly heterogeneous populations.
evidence: Directly stated comparison of regional heterogeneity.

claim: Newly collected samples reinforce previous findings of high heterogeneity in Rome, including a large portion of the population having affinities for present-day Near Eastern populations.
source: Newly collected samples reinforce previous findings of high heterogeneity in Rome, including a large portion of the population having affinities for present-day Near Eastern populations (Antonio et al., 2019; Posth et al., 2021; Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Stated with citations and reference to figure.

claim: Southeastern European and Western European individuals during the Imperial Roman & Late Antiquity period exhibit high heterogeneity, on par with that of contemporaneous Italy.
source: Interestingly, Southeastern European and Western European individuals during the Imperial Roman & Late Antiquity period also exhibit high heterogeneity, on par with that of contemporaneous Italy (Figures 3 and 4).
evidence: Stated with reference to Figures 3 and 4.

claim: In Southeastern Europe, a core group of individuals have ancestry similar to that of present-day and contemporaneous Central Europeans (C6).
source: In Southeastern Europe, a core group of individuals have ancestry similar to that of present-day and contemporaneous Central Europeans (C6), while other clusters have ancestry similar to that of Northern Europeans (C7) and Eastern Mediterraneans (C8) (Figure 3C).
evidence: Stated with reference to Figure 3C showing PCA.

claim: In Southeastern Europe, other clusters have ancestry similar to that of Northern Europeans (C7) and Eastern Mediterraneans (C8).
source: In Southeastern Europe, a core group of individuals have ancestry similar to that of present-day and contemporaneous Central Europeans (C6), while other clusters have ancestry similar to that of Northern Europeans (C7) and Eastern Mediterraneans (C8) (Figure 3C).
evidence: Stated with reference to Figure 3C.

claim: These ancestry groups (Central European, Northern European, Eastern Mediterranean) are found in contemporaneous Italy and Western Europe as well.
source: These ancestry groups are found in contemporaneous Italy and Western Europe as well (Figure 4C, Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Stated with reference to figures.

claim: Individuals of eastern nomadic ancestry, similar to that of Sarmatian individuals, were observed in both Western Europe (C8, n=2) and Southeastern Europe (C2, n=2).
source: We also observe individuals of eastern nomadic ancestry, similar to that of Sarmatian individuals previously reported, in both Western Europe (C8, n=2) and Southeastern Europe (C2, n=2).
evidence: Directly stated observation with sample counts.

claim: 11% of individuals were identified as outliers.
source: In total, we identified 11% of individuals as outliers, and could connect 7% of individuals to a putative source in a different region (Figure 5A).
evidence: Directly stated percentage from outlier analysis.

claim: 7% of individuals could be connected to a putative source in a different region.
source: In total, we identified 11% of individuals as outliers, and could connect 7% of individuals to a putative source in a different region (Figure 5A).
evidence: Directly stated percentage from source modeling.

claim: No outliers were found within Armenia.
source: Unsurprisingly, no outliers were found within Armenia; however, we found outlier individuals in the Levant and Italy who can be putatively traced back to Armenia according to their ancestry (Figure 5C; blue outgoing arrows from Armenia).
evidence: Directly stated result of outlier analysis.

claim: Outlier individuals in the Levant and Italy can be putatively traced back to Armenia according to their ancestry.
source: Unsurprisingly, no outliers were found within Armenia; however, we found outlier individuals in the Levant and Italy who can be putatively traced back to Armenia according to their ancestry (Figure 5C; blue outgoing arrows from Armenia).
evidence: Stated with reference to Figure 5C showing network.

claim: Outliers found in Iron Age Tunisia indicate movements from many regions in Europe.
source: In North Africa, outliers found in Iron Age Tunisia (Moots et al., 2022) indicate movements from many regions in Europe, and North African-like outliers were found in Italy and Austria (Western Europe).
evidence: Stated with citation to Moots et al., 2022.

claim: North African-like outliers were found in Italy and Austria (Western Europe).
source: In North Africa, outliers found in Iron Age Tunisia (Moots et al., 2022) indicate movements from many regions in Europe, and North African-like outliers were found in Italy and Austria (Western Europe).
evidence: Directly stated observation.

claim: North African ancestry in Italy is supported by a single previously reported individual from the Imperial Roman period (R132).
source: North African ancestry in Italy is supported by a single previously reported individual from the Imperial Roman period (R132; Antonio et al., 2019).
evidence: Stated with citation to Antonio et al., 2019.

claim: Similar North African ancestry in Western Europe is supported by a single individual, R10667, from Wels, Austria.
source: Similar North African ancestry in Western Europe is supported by a single individual, R10667, from Wels, Austria, a site located on the frontier of the Roman Empire (C28 in Figure 4).
evidence: Directly stated with reference to Figure 4.

claim: Individual R10667 from Wels, Austria can be modeled using Canary Islander individuals from the Medieval Ages or an Iron Age outlier from Kerkouane, Tunisia.
source: This individual from Austria can be modeled using Canary Islander individuals from the Medieval Ages or an Iron Age outlier (distinguished by having more sub-Saharan ancestry) from Kerkouane, a Punic city near Carthage in modern-day Tunisia.
evidence: Directly stated result of admixture modeling.

claim: The 7% estimate for outliers with source should be considered conservative for the proportion of 'non-local' individuals.
source: The 7% estimate for outliers with source should be considered conservative for the proportion of 'non-local' individuals.
evidence: Explicitly stated interpretation of results.

claim: There is a large decrease in overall FST from the Mesolithic & Neolithic periods to the Bronze Age (approximately 10,000–2300 BCE), coinciding with the major prehistoric migrations.
source: Across time periods, we see a large decrease in overall FST from the Mesolithic & Neolithic periods to the Bronze Age (approximately 10,000–2300 BCE), coinciding with the major prehistoric migrations (Haak et al., 2015; Lazaridis et al., 2014).
evidence: Stated with citations to major prehistoric migration studies.

claim: From the Bronze Age onward, FST does not decrease further with time, indicating that the level of genetic differentiation across space is relatively stable from the Bronze Age to present-day.
source: From the Bronze Age onward, however, FST does not decrease further with time, indicating that the level of genetic differentiation across space is relatively stable from the Bronze Age to present-day.
evidence: Directly stated interpretation of FST analysis.

claim: Historical period genomes show similar spatial structure to present-day genomes, although noisier due to a narrower sampling distribution and higher local genetic heterogeneity.
source: Echoing close correspondence between genetic structure and geographic space in present-day Europeans (Novembre et al., 2008), we recovered similar spatial structure for historical samples as well, although noisier due to a narrower sampling distribution and higher local genetic heterogeneity (Figure 6B, middle).
evidence: Stated with reference to Figure 6B and citation.

claim: The similarity in structure between present-day and historical period is especially striking in comparison to a projection of prehistoric genomes, which shows much weaker correspondence to the present-day PCA as well as to geographic space.
source: The similarity in structure between present-day and historical period is especially striking in comparison to a projection of prehistoric genomes, which shows much weaker correspondence to the present-day PCA as well as to geographic space (Figure 6B, top).
evidence: Stated with reference to Figure 6B showing PCA projections.

claim: European and Mediterranean population structure has been relatively stable over the last 3000 years.
source: Together, our analyses indicate that European and Mediterranean population structure has been relatively stable over the last 3000 years.
evidence: Directly stated conclusion from FST and PCA analyses.

claim: In simulations with long-range dispersal as low as 4%, FST decreases over 120 generations (~3000 years with a generation time of 25 years).
source: Even with long-range dispersal as low as 4%, we observe decreasing FST over 120 generations (~3000 years with a generation time of 25 years) as individuals become less differentiated genetically across space (Figure 7B).
evidence: Directly stated simulation result with reference to Figure 7B.

claim: At 8% long-range dispersal, FST decreases dramatically within 120 generations as spatial structure collapses to the point that it is hardly detectable in the first two principal components.
source: At 8%, FST decreases dramatically within 120 generations as spatial structure collapses to the point that it is hardly detectable in the first two principal components (Figure 7C).
evidence: Directly stated simulation result with reference to Figure 7C.

claim: Under a basic spatial population genetics model, we would expect structure to collapse by present-day given the levels of movement observed.
source: These simulations indicate that under a basic spatial population genetics model we would expect structure to collapse by present-day given the levels of movement we observe.
evidence: Directly stated interpretation of simulation results.

claim: Overall population structure across western Eurasia is relatively stable through the historical period up to the present, mirroring geography.
source: Despite this high level of mobility, overall population structure across western Eurasia is relatively stable through the historical period up to the present, mirroring geography.
evidence: Directly stated in the abstract as a main finding.

claim: At least 7% of historical individuals carry ancestry uncommon in the region where they were sampled, some indicating cross-Mediterranean contacts.
source: At least 7% of historical individuals carry ancestry uncommon in the region where they were sampled, some indicating cross-Mediterranean contacts.
evidence: Directly stated in the abstract as a main finding.

claim: Under standard population genetics models with local panmixia, the observed level of dispersal would lead to a collapse of population structure.
source: We show that, under standard population genetics models with local panmixia, the observed level of dispersal would lead to a collapse of population structure.
evidence: Directly stated in the abstract as a main finding from simulations.

claim: Persistent population structure suggests a lower effective migration rate than indicated by the observed dispersal.
source: Persistent population structure thus suggests a lower effective migration rate than indicated by the observed dispersal.
evidence: Directly stated inference in the abstract.

claim: The phenomenon of stable structure despite high mobility can be explained by extensive transient dispersal arising from drastically improved transportation networks and the Roman Empire's mobilization of people for trade, labor, and military.
source: We hypothesize that this phenomenon can be explained by extensive transient dispersal arising from drastically improved transportation networks and the Roman Empire's mobilization of people for trade, labor, and military.
evidence: Directly stated hypothesis in the abstract.

claim: Dates for 126 samples were directly determined through radiocarbon dating.
source: Dates for 126 samples were directly determined through radiocarbon dating, and were used alongside archaeological contexts to infer dates for the remaining samples.
evidence: Directly stated in methods section.

claim: Libraries were partially treated with uracil-DNA glycosylase (UDG).
source: Libraries were partially treated with uracil-DNA glycosylase (UDG) and screened for ancient DNA damage patterns, high endogenous DNA content, and low contamination.
evidence: Directly stated in methods section.

claim: The major ancestry components of present-day west Eurasians were largely established by the end of the Bronze Age.
source: Given that the major ancestry components of present-day west Eurasians were largely established by the end of the Bronze Age, it is unclear how and what types of demographic processes impacted the genetic make-up of western Eurasia over the last ~3000 years, from the end of the Bronze Age to present-day.
evidence: Stated as established knowledge in the introduction.

claim: The farming transition occurred around 7500 BCE.
source: Prehistoric ancient genomes have allowed disentangling the movements of people and technologies across two major demographic transitions in prehistoric western Eurasia: first the farming transition ~7500 BCE (Lazaridis et al., 2014; Skoglund et al., 2012), and later the Bronze Age Steppe migrations ~3500 BCE (Haak et al., 2015).
evidence: Stated with citations to key studies.

claim: The Bronze Age Steppe migrations occurred around 3500 BCE.
source: Prehistoric ancient genomes have allowed disentangling the movements of people and technologies across two major demographic transitions in prehistoric western Eurasia: first the farming transition ~7500 BCE (Lazaridis et al., 2014; Skoglund et al., 2012), and later the Bronze Age Steppe migrations ~3500 BCE (Haak et al., 2015).
evidence: Stated with citation to Haak et al., 2015.

claim: In prehistoric times, migrations would take hundreds of years to traverse the continent.
source: For the spread of Farmer and Steppe ancestry, we know that these prehistoric migrations would take hundreds of years to traverse the continent (Allentoft et al., 2015; Haak et al., 2015; Lazaridis et al., 2016).
evidence: Stated with citations to multiple studies.

claim: In the historical period, there were dense travel networks of roads and waterways as well as clear incentives for cross-Mediterranean and cross-continental movement.
source: In contrast, in the historical period, there were dense travel networks of roads and waterways as well as clear incentives for cross-Mediterranean and cross-continental movement (Abulafia, 2011; Beard, 2015; Broodbank, 2013; Symonds, 2017).
evidence: Stated with citations to historical sources.

claim: In the historical period, people could travel cross-continental distances on the order of weeks or months, well within their lifetimes.
source: This enabled people to travel cross-continental distances on the order of weeks or months, well within their lifetimes (Figure 5—figure supplements 2 and 3; Scheidel, 2015).
evidence: Stated with reference to figures and citation.

claim: During the expansion of the Roman Empire, existing and new cities quickly expanded as hubs for trade and labor.
source: During the expansion of the Empire, existing and new cities quickly expanded as hubs for trade and labor.
evidence: Stated as historical context.

claim: Urban-military complexes emerged along the frontier as military forces established themselves and drew in local communities which sought protection or economic benefit.
source: Urban-military complexes emerged along the frontier as military forces established themselves and drew in local communities which sought protection or economic benefit (Verhagen et al., 2019).
evidence: Stated with citation to Verhagen et al., 2019.

claim: According to the Urban Graveyard Effect hypothesis, the influx of migrants in city-centers disproportionately contributed to the death rate over the birth rate.
source: According to a longstanding historical hypothesis, the Urban Graveyard Effect, the influx of migrants in city-centers disproportionately contributed to the death rate over the birth rate; a process which would contribute to observing individuals as 'transient' migrants (Tacoma, 2016).
evidence: Stated with citation to Tacoma, 2016.

claim: The collapse of the Empire involved a loss of urban-military complexes and depopulation of cities, followed by ruralization.
source: The collapse of the Empire involved a loss of urban-military complexes and depopulation of cities, followed by ruralization (Burgess, 2007; Dey, 2015; Roymans et al., 2020).
evidence: Stated with citations to historical sources.

claim: Ancient DNA comes from archaeological excavations, which tend to be enriched in urban areas.
source: The lack of samples is further amplified by the fact that ancient DNA comes from archaeological excavations, which tend to be enriched in urban areas; a stone mausoleum in the city center, for example, will produce more surface scatter than a wood farmhouse, making urban areas more likely for excavation (Bowes, 2011).
evidence: Stated with citation to Bowes, 2011.

claim: The proportions of males and females do not differ significantly between outlier and non-outlier groups (p=0.4117).
source: Among the outliers identified, we did not find a significant sex bias compared to non-outliers. Overall, there are more males than females in the dataset. However, the proportions of males in non-outliers, outliers with source, and outliers without source do not differ significantly by a Chi-squared test (p-value = 0.4117, df = 2; Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Directly stated statistical test result with reference to figure.

claim: When outliers (with and without source) are treated as one group, there is still no significant association with outlier status and sex (p=0.633).
source: When outliers (with and without source) are treated as one group, there is still no significant association with outlier status and sex (p-value = 0.633, df = 1).
evidence: Directly stated statistical test result.

claim: In each time period, the classical pattern of isolation-by-distance was recovered, where individuals closer in geographic space are also more similar genetically.
source: In each time period, we recovered the classical pattern of isolation-by-distance (Figure 6A), where individuals closer in geographic space are also more similar genetically.
evidence: Directly stated result with reference to Figure 6A.

claim: The study hypothesizes that both the loss of transient migrants and repopulation by less heterogeneous, but temporally stable, local populations could have helped maintain overall stability of genetic structure from the Iron Age to present-day.
source: Based on genetic analyses and the rich historical record, we hypothesize that both the loss of transient migrants which contributed to population heterogeneity, as well as repopulation by less heterogeneous, but temporally stable, local populations could have helped maintain overall stability of genetic structure from the Iron Age to present-day.
evidence: Directly stated hypothesis in the discussion.

claim: In the historical period there was an increasing decoupling of movement and reproduction, compared to prehistoric times.
source: We hypothesize that in the historical period there was an increasing decoupling of movement and reproduction, compared to prehistoric times.
evidence: Directly stated hypothesis in the discussion.

claim: In the simulated populations, migration implies both movement and reproduction with local random mate choice.
source: In the simulated populations, migration implies both movement and reproduction with local random mate choice.
evidence: Directly stated description of simulation assumptions.

claim: In real human populations migration can be more complex: people do not necessarily reproduce where they migrate, and reproduction is not necessarily random.
source: However, in real human populations migration can be more complex: people do not necessarily reproduce where they migrate, and reproduction is not necessarily random.
evidence: Directly stated contrast between simulations and reality.

claim: Sampling was performed to maximize coverage across Europe and the Mediterranean, as opposed to detailed site level sampling.
source: Sampling was performed to maximize coverage across Europe and the Mediterranean, as opposed to detailed site level sampling.
evidence: Directly stated sampling strategy.

claim: The study particularly focused on regions where there was no published genomic data for the Imperial Roman and Late Antiquity Period at the time of sampling (e.g. France, Austria, the Balkans, Armenia, and North Africa).
source: We particularly focused on regions where there was no published genomic data for the Imperial Roman and Late Antiquity Period at the time of sampling (e.g. France, Austria, the Balkans, Armenia, and North Africa).
evidence: Directly stated sampling focus.

claim: One gram of petrous bone was sent for radiocarbon dating by Accelerator Mass Spectrometry (AMS) at the Keck Carbon Cycle AMS Facility at the University of California, Irvine.
source: For each sample, one gram of petrous bone was sent for radiocarbon dating by Accelerator Mass Spectrometry (AMS) at the Keck Carbon Cycle AMS Facility at the University of California, Irvine.
evidence: Directly stated methods for radiocarbon dating.

claim: The cochlear regions of the petrous bones were isolated and finely ground in dedicated clean room facilities at the University of Vienna.
source: We isolated and finely ground the cochlear regions of the petrous bones in dedicated clean room facilities at the University of Vienna following the protocols described in Pinhasi et al., 2019; Pinhasi et al., 2015.
evidence: Directly stated methods with citations.

claim: Using 50 mg of bone powder, DNA was extracted by 18 hr incubation of the powder in a solution of Proteinase-K and EDTA.
source: Using 50 mg of bone powder, DNA was extracted by 18 hr incubation of the powder in a solution of Proteinase-K and EDTA.
evidence: Directly stated extraction protocol.

claim: Samples were screened and selected using criteria including >20% reads aligned to the hg19 build of the human genome.
source: Samples were screened and selected using the following criteria: (1)>20% reads aligned to the hg19 build of the human genome; (2) a C>T mismatch rate at the 5'-end and G>A at the 3'-end of the sequencing read of 4% or above (characterized with mapDamage v2.0.8) (Jónsson et al., 2013); (3) library complexity estimates indicating that a minimum coverage of 0.5 x would be achievable with further sequencing, (4) with a contamination level ≤ 5%.
evidence: Directly stated screening criteria.

claim: Samples with contamination estimate above 5% for any of three methods were considered contaminated and excluded from downstream analysis (n=9).
source: If the contamination estimate for any of these three methods was above 5%, we considered the sample contaminated and excluded it from downstream analysis (n=9).
evidence: Directly stated exclusion criteria and number excluded.

claim: The 204 new samples that passed quality filters have a median genome-wide depth of 0.92 x (0.16x to 2.38x).
source: For passing samples, processed data from all sequencing runs were merged into a single BAM file. The 204 new samples that passed quality filters have a median genome-wide depth of 0.92 x (0.16x to 2.38x).
evidence: Directly stated sequencing depth statistics.

claim: Principal component analysis was performed on genotypes from present-day and Mediterranean individuals using smartpca v16000.
source: Principal component analysis was performed on genotypes from present-day and Mediterranean individuals using smartpca v16000 (https://github.com/chrchang/eigensoft/blob/master/POPGEN/README; Chang, 2013).
evidence: Directly stated methods with software version and citation.

claim: After outlier removal, 829 individuals and 480,712 SNPs were used in the initial PCA analysis.
source: After outlier removal (which removed 55 samples), 829 individuals and 480,712 SNPs were used in the initial analysis.
evidence: Directly stated sample and SNP counts for PCA.

claim: FST was calculated between groups of individuals on a sliding spatial grid, with each grid cell measuring 10 degrees longitude by 10 degrees latitude.
source: To assess the extent of genetic differentiation across geographic space within a time period, we calculated the Fixation index (FST) between groups of individuals on a sliding spatial grid. Each grid cell measured 10 degrees longitude by 10 degrees latitude, and was slid by 1 degree in both directions (north and east) nine times to build a total of 10 spatial grids.
evidence: Directly stated methods for FST calculation.

claim: Pairwise FST was calculated between all populated grid cells using Hudson's estimator, correcting for unequal sample size.
source: For each of these grids, pairwise FST was calculated between all populated 10-by-10 grid cells using Hudson's estimator, correcting for unequal sample size (Bhatia et al., 2013).
evidence: Directly stated methods with citation.

claim: The study used qpAdm tool of admixtools 2.0 to build a workflow for ancestry modeling and outlier identification.
source: We used the qpAdm tool of admixtools 2.0 to build a workflow that:
evidence: Directly stated methods.

claim: Hierarchical clustering was performed using the UPGMA algorithm as implemented in python's scipy.cluster.hierarchy (v. 1.6.1).
source: To cluster individuals into groups of genetically similar individuals, we performed hierarchical clustering on the dissimilarity matrix constructed from all pairwise values of d within a region. Hierarchical clustering was performed using the UPGMA algorithm as implemented in python's scipy.cluster.hierarchy (v. 1.6.1).
evidence: Directly stated methods with software version.

claim: The hierarchical clustering was split into flat clusters using a dissimilarity cutoff of 1.3, which corresponds to a nominal p-value cutoff of 0.05.
source: The hierarchical clustering was then split into flat clusters using a dissimilarity cutoff of 1.3, which corresponds to a nominal p-value cutoff of 0.05.
evidence: Directly stated clustering threshold.

claim: Clusters consisting of less than 5% of the total population or no more than two individuals in the region were classified as outlier candidates.
source: Clusters consisting of less than 5% of the total population or no more than two individuals in the region (across time) were classified as outlier candidates, whose ancestry is underrepresented in the region they were sampled.
evidence: Directly stated outlier classification criteria.

claim: Forward simulations in continuous 2D space were set up using SLiM v. 3.6.
source: To assess how spatial population structure would be impacted by different modes of dispersal, we set up forward simulations in continuous 2D space using SLiM v. 3.6 (Haller and Messer, 2019).
evidence: Directly stated simulation methods with software version and citation.

claim: The simulations used diploid genomes made up of a single, 10^8 bp long chromosome, with recombination rate and mutation rate set to 10^-8.
source: We simulated diploid genomes made up of a single, 108 bp long chromosome, with recombination rate and mutation rate set to 10–8.
evidence: Directly stated simulation parameters.

claim: The population evolved forward in time for 2000+120 generations during which spatial population structure was established.
